question:
Identify the grammatical error in the following sentence and select the correct tense from the options given below.
I have met my friend yesterday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. met my friend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "I have met my friend yesterday" wrongly combines the Present Perfect Tense (have + V3) with the time expression "yesterday", which is reserved for the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule: Words/phrases that refer to a definite, finished point of time in the past such as yesterday, last week, in 2010, ago always require the Simple Past Tense (Subject + V2), never the Present Perfect Tense.

• Applying the rule, "have met" must be changed to the simple past form "met", giving the correct sentence: I met my friend yesterday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "had been meeting" is incorrect because this is the Past Perfect Continuous form, used for an action continuing up to a point in the past, it does not fit a single completed action with "yesterday".

• Option 2: "was meeting" is incorrect because this is the Past Continuous form, which describes an action in progress at a specific past moment, not a simple completed action.

• Option 4: "have been meeting" is incorrect because this is the Present Perfect Continuous form; like the original sentence, it clashes with the definite past time marker "yesterday".

NOTE

• Present Perfect Tense (have/has + V3) is used for actions with no definite time in the past, or actions connecting the past to the present, e.g. "I have already met him" (correct) versus "I have met him yesterday" (incorrect).

• Other definite past time markers that require Simple Past: last night, in 1998, the other day, once upon a time.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The teacher was / taken back by / the audacity of / the new student.
A B C D
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. B.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Segment B, "taken back by", contains the error. The correct idiomatic expression is "taken aback by", not "taken back by".

• Rule Fixed idiomatic expression: "Taken aback (by/at)" is a fixed phrase meaning to be surprised or shocked. The word "aback" (not "back") is the only correct form used in this idiom; "taken back" is a common but incorrect confusion based on sound.

• Applying the correction: The teacher was taken aback by the audacity of the new student.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 (Segment B).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (Segment D, "the new student") is grammatically and idiomatically correct; it simply names the subject causing the audacity.

• Option 2 (Segment C, "the audacity of") is correct as written; "audacity" (boldness/impudence) is used appropriately with the preposition "of".

• Option 3 (Segment A, "The teacher was") is a correct subject plus auxiliary verb construction and contains no error by itself.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "taken aback" (surprised) with "taken back", which is not a standard idiom in this sense (though "take somebody back" can separately mean to remind someone of an earlier time, e.g. "This song takes me back to my childhood").

• Other commonly confused sound-alike idiom errors tested by SSC: "in the offing" (not "in the offering"), "could care less" (should be "couldn't care less"), "for all intents and purposes" (not "intensive purposes").

question:
Select the most appropriate article to fill in the blank.
_________ bed you sleep in is broken.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank refers to one particular, specific bed, identified precisely by the relative clause "...you sleep in", and not to beds in general.

• Rule Definite Article "The": "The" is used before a noun when the speaker and listener both know exactly which one is being referred to, especially when the noun is followed by a defining/restrictive clause (e.g. "the book you gave me", "the bed you sleep in").

• Applying the rule, the sentence must begin with "The bed you sleep in is broken."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("A") and Option 4 ("An") are incorrect because indefinite articles are used for any one, non specific member of a class, whereas here a specific, already identified bed is meant. "An" would also be wrong before the consonant sound of "bed" in any case.

• Option 2 ("On") is incorrect because "on" is a preposition, not an article, and cannot grammatically begin the sentence in place of an article before the noun "bed".

NOTE

• Use "the" for nouns made specific by a following defining clause, a superlative, or when there is only one of something (e.g. "the sun", "the Prime Minister of India").

• Use "a/an" for the first mention of a countable noun or when referring to any one member of a class, not a particular one.

question:
Select the option that will improve the given sentence by using the most appropriate verb.
That Macbook belong to Xavier.
option_1: That Macbook is belonged to Xavier.
option_4: That Macbook is belong to Xavier.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That Macbook belongs to Xavier.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "That Macbook" is a third person singular subject, so the verb must take the "-s/-es" ending in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule Subject Verb Agreement in Simple Present Tense: With a third person singular subject (he/she/it or a singular noun), the base verb must add -s or -es: e.g. "he belongs", "she runs", "it belongs".

• Applying the rule, "belong" must become "belongs", giving: That Macbook belongs to Xavier.

• Additionally, "belong" is a stative/non continuous verb (expressing a state of possession, not an action), so it is never used in the passive voice or continuous tense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "is belonged to" is incorrect because "belong" is a stative verb and cannot be used in the passive voice.

• Option 3: "belonging to" is incorrect because it lacks a finite (main) verb, "belonging" alone is a participle and cannot complete the sentence grammatically.

• Option 4: "is belong to" is incorrect because it wrongly combines the auxiliary "is" with the base form "belong", which is not a valid verb structure.

NOTE

• Other common stative verbs that are never used in continuous or passive forms: know, own, possess, resemble, prefer, believe, seem, want.

• Remember the -s/-es rule also applies to verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o (e.g. "wishes", "goes", "catches").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

It is generally (1)________that the methodology of teaching-learning is the concern of teachers only. Learners have (2) ____or nothing to do with it. But this is not true. The teaching-learning (3) ______ are concerns of learners as well. Knowing and understanding that how different subjects are taught are important for the learners of all subjects, but it has more (4) ______for the learners of physical education. When we talk about you as learners of physical education, we mean that you have actually participated in the subject area, rather than (5) ______studied it.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. believed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the structure **"It is generally _____ that..."**, which is a common fixed collocation used to introduce a widely held opinion or notion.

• Rule Collocation: The phrase "It is generally believed that..." is a standard formal expression meaning "most people think/hold the opinion that...". "Believed" collocates naturally with "generally" in this reporting structure.

• Applying this to the passage: "It is generally believed that the methodology of teaching-learning is the concern of teachers only.", this fits the sense of a common (though mistaken) opinion, which the passage goes on to correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hoped" is incorrect because "hope" expresses a wish for a future outcome, not a present belief/opinion about a fact.

• Option 2: "wished" is incorrect for the same reason, "wish" expresses desire, not a widely held opinion.

• Option 3: "planned" is incorrect because "planned" refers to a deliberate future arrangement, which does not fit the context of a commonly held view.

NOTE

• Other similar formal reporting collocations frequently tested by SSC: "It is widely believed that...", "It is often argued that...", "It is generally accepted/assumed that..."

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

It is generally (1)________that the methodology of teaching-learning is the concern of teachers only. Learners have (2) ____or nothing to do with it. But this is not true. The teaching-learning (3) ______ are concerns of learners as well. Knowing and understanding that how different subjects are taught are important for the learners of all subjects, but it has more (4) ______for the learners of physical education. When we talk about you as learners of physical education, we mean that you have actually participated in the subject area, rather than (5) ______studied it.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. little.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in the fixed expression "have little or nothing to do with", meaning to have almost no connection or involvement with something.

• Rule Fixed Idiomatic Collocation: "Little or nothing" is a set phrase used to emphasise a very small (almost negligible) amount, paired here with "or nothing" to reinforce the sense of minimal involvement.

• Applying this to the passage: "Learners have little or nothing to do with it" means learners are seen (wrongly) as having almost no role in the teaching-learning methodology.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "light" is incorrect because "light" describes weight or brightness, not quantity/degree of involvement, and does not collocate with "or nothing".

• Option 2: "minute" is incorrect because although "minute" (pronounced my-NEWT) can mean "tiny", it does not fit the fixed expression "____ or nothing to do with".

• Option 4: "sparse" is incorrect because "sparse" describes something thinly scattered or spread out, not a small degree of connection, and does not collocate with "or nothing".

NOTE

• The construction "[quantifier] or nothing" is common in formal English: "little or nothing", "few or no [plural noun]", always check for such fixed pairings in cloze passages.

• Do not confuse "little" (small amount, used with uncountable nouns) with "few" (small number, used with countable nouns).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

It is generally (1)________that the methodology of teaching-learning is the concern of teachers only. Learners have (2) ____or nothing to do with it. But this is not true. The teaching-learning (3) ______ are concerns of learners as well. Knowing and understanding that how different subjects are taught are important for the learners of all subjects, but it has more (4) ______for the learners of physical education. When we talk about you as learners of physical education, we mean that you have actually participated in the subject area, rather than (5) ______studied it.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. methods.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun referring to the ways/techniques of teaching-learning, since the passage discusses "the methodology of teaching-learning" earlier and repeats the idea as "the teaching-learning _____".

• Rule Contextual/Topical Vocabulary: In a cloze passage, the missing word must match the topic established earlier in the passage. Since the opening line already refers to "methodology", the blank should be filled with a word from the same semantic field, "methods".

• Applying this to the passage: "The teaching-learning methods are concerns of learners as well.", this directly echoes and restates "methodology" in simpler terms.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "forms" is incorrect because "forms" refers to shapes/types/documents, not specifically to techniques of teaching.

• Option 2: "breaks" is incorrect because "breaks" means pauses or interruptions, which is unrelated to the context of teaching methodology.

• Option 3: "customs" is incorrect because "customs" refers to traditional social practices, not teaching techniques, and does not fit the academic context.

NOTE

• When solving cloze passages, always scan the surrounding sentences (not just the immediate blank) for repeated or related keywords, here "methodology" earlier in the passage is the strongest clue for "methods".

• Related words often confused in vocabulary based cloze passages: method (a way of doing something), custom (a traditional practice), form (a shape/type), habit (a repeated personal practice).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

It is generally (1)________that the methodology of teaching-learning is the concern of teachers only. Learners have (2) ____or nothing to do with it. But this is not true. The teaching-learning (3) ______ are concerns of learners as well. Knowing and understanding that how different subjects are taught are important for the learners of all subjects, but it has more (4) ______for the learners of physical education. When we talk about you as learners of physical education, we mean that you have actually participated in the subject area, rather than (5) ______studied it.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. relevance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word meaning importance/significance, since the sentence contrasts general importance for "learners of all subjects" with something greater, **"more _____ for the learners of physical education"**.

• Rule Contextual Word Choice: The sentence structure "it has more X for the learners of physical education" (contrasted with general importance for all subjects) calls for a word meaning special significance or applicability, which is exactly what "relevance" means.

• Applying this to the passage: "...it has more relevance for the learners of physical education", meaning the subject is more directly applicable/significant to them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "reference" is incorrect because "reference" means a mention or source of information, not significance/importance.

• Option 2: "recurrence" is incorrect because "recurrence" means happening again, which does not fit the sense of importance intended here.

• Option 4: "consistency" is incorrect because "consistency" refers to being uniform or unchanging, not to significance or applicability.

NOTE

• "Relevance" (noun) and "relevant" (adjective) are frequently tested, e.g. "This point is highly relevant to our discussion."

• Do not confuse "relevance" (importance/applicability) with "reverence" (deep respect), a common SSC distractor pair.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

It is generally (1)________that the methodology of teaching-learning is the concern of teachers only. Learners have (2) ____or nothing to do with it. But this is not true. The teaching-learning (3) ______ are concerns of learners as well. Knowing and understanding that how different subjects are taught are important for the learners of all subjects, but it has more (4) ______for the learners of physical education. When we talk about you as learners of physical education, we mean that you have actually participated in the subject area, rather than (5) ______studied it.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. merely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank contrasts actual participation with just reading about/studying the subject, "rather than (merely) studied it", so the missing word must mean "only/simply", emphasising the limited nature of mere study compared to actual participation.

• Rule Contextual Adverb Choice: "Merely" means "only, simply, no more than", and fits naturally in contrastive structures like "not just X but Y" or "rather than merely X".

• Applying this to the passage: "...you have actually participated in the subject area, rather than merely studied it.", the contrast between "actually participated" and "merely studied" is completed correctly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "hardly" is incorrect because "hardly" means "almost not at all", which changes the intended meaning to suggest studying barely happened, rather than emphasising its limited value compared to participation.

• Option 3: "purely" is incorrect because "purely" means "entirely/solely" and is typically used for describing motives or composition (e.g. "purely academic"), not natural in this contrastive structure.

• Option 4: "entirely" is incorrect because "entirely" means "completely", which does not fit the sense of a limited/insufficient action being contrasted with actual participation.

NOTE

• "Merely" is a very common SSC cloze-passage word used to downplay or limit an action, often paired with contrastive structures like "not merely... but also..." or "rather than merely...".

• Do not confuse "hardly" (almost not) with "hardy" (tough, able to endure difficult conditions), a common spelling confusion.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
On its last legs
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. In a bad condition.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "On its last legs" means to be in a very poor, worn out, or failing condition, close to breaking down or ceasing to function/exist. (बहुत खराब हालत में / अंतिम सांसें गिनना)
◦ Example: The old washing machine is on its last legs; we'll need to replace it soon.

• The expression originally referred to a person or animal so exhausted that it could barely stand on its own legs, and was later extended figuratively to machines, institutions, and relationships that are about to fail.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Creeping on legs" is a literal, non idiomatic description and does not capture the figurative meaning of decline or failure.

• Option 2: "Last choice" incorrectly relates "last" to a preference or ranking rather than to physical/functional decline.

• Option 3: "Slow movement" describes pace, not the state of being worn out or near collapse, and so misses the idiom's true sense.

NOTE

• Related idioms of decline/failure often asked in SSC: "on the rocks" (in serious trouble, especially a relationship), "hanging by a thread" (in a very precarious/risky state), and "go downhill" (to deteriorate progressively).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
The upshot of the consultation with the doctor was an operation scheduled for the next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Cause.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Upshot" means the final outcome, result, or conclusion of a discussion or a series of events. (परिणाम/निष्कर्ष)
◦ Example: The upshot of the meeting was a complete change in company policy.

• Since "upshot" means an effect or result, its antonym must mean the opposite, that which produces the effect, i.e. "Cause".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Blame" means responsibility for a fault; it is unrelated to the cause-effect relationship being tested here.

• Option 3: "Result" is incorrect because it is a synonym, not an antonym, of "upshot", both mean the outcome of something.

• Option 4: "Estimate" means an approximate calculation or judgment; it does not form a direct opposite of "upshot".

NOTE

• Remember the cause and effect word pairs commonly tested as antonyms: cause vs effect/result/outcome/upshot/consequence.

• Other synonyms of "upshot": outcome, consequence, conclusion, culmination.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiomatic expression that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.:
It feels like I made a promise of more than my ability when I promised to complete this worksheet in one day.
option_3: bit off more than I could chew
option_4: burnt a hole in my pocket
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. bit off more than I could chew.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To bite off more than one can chew" means to take on or promise more responsibility/work than one is actually capable of handling. (अपनी क्षमता से अधिक का जिम्मा लेना)
◦ Example: By agreeing to organise the entire event alone, she bit off more than she could chew.

• The underlined phrase "made a promise of more than my ability" exactly describes promising to do more than one's capability allows, matching the idiom's meaning precisely.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "beat my brain out" (बहुत दिमाग लगाना): To think very hard about something; it refers to mental effort, not over-promising.

• Option 2: "beat the drum" (किसी बात का खूब प्रचार करना): To publicly promote or draw attention to something; unrelated to overestimating one's ability.

• Option 4: "burnt a hole in my pocket" (बहुत पैसा खर्च करना): Used when money is spent very quickly/carelessly; it concerns finances, not overcommitment of ability.

NOTE

• Other idioms about overcommitment/capability often asked in SSC: "to have too many irons in the fire" (to be involved in too many things at once) and "to spread oneself too thin" (to take on too many tasks to do any of them well).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
It will take two hours to walk across the forest.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. through.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes walking from one side of the forest to the other, passing within/inside it, this sense of movement within a three-dimensional or enclosed space is expressed by the preposition "through", not "across".

• Rule Prepositions of Movement: "Across" is properly used for movement over a flat, open surface (e.g. "walk across the road/field"), while "through" is used for movement within an enclosed space that one enters and exits (e.g. "walk through the forest/tunnel/crowd").

• Applying the rule: since a forest is a dense, enclosed area one walks inside rather than merely over, "through" is the more precise substitute: It will take two hours to walk through the forest.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "over" is incorrect because "over" implies movement above or on top of something, which does not fit walking inside a forest.

• Option 3: "away" is incorrect because "away" indicates distance/departure from a place, not the notion of passing through it.

• Option 4: "between" is incorrect because "between" indicates a position or movement relative to two distinct points/objects, which does not match "walking a forest".

NOTE

• Preposition pairs commonly tested by SSC: across (a flat/open surface) vs through (an enclosed space); over (above/on top of) vs under (below).

• Other examples: "swim across the river" (surface), "walk through the tunnel" (enclosed), "climb over the wall" (on top of).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The wizard, while performing an item, accidentally set his own hat on fire and prompted the fire alarm to go on.
option_1: the fire alarm to go away
option_2: the fire alarm to go under
option_3: the fire alarm to go off
option_4: the fire alarm to go above
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. the fire alarm to go off.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct phrasal verb for an alarm, bell, or siren starting to sound/activate is "go off", not "go on".

• Rule Fixed Phrasal Verb: "Go off" (in the context of alarms, bombs, and fireworks) means to be triggered or to start making a loud noise suddenly. "Go on" instead usually means to continue happening or to be switched on (as with a light), which does not fit an alarm being triggered.

• Applying the rule: "...accidentally set his own hat on fire and prompted the fire alarm to go off."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "go away" is incorrect because it means to leave or disappear, which is not what an alarm does when triggered.

• Option 2: "go under" is incorrect because this phrasal verb means to fail or sink (e.g. a business going under), unrelated to an alarm sounding.

• Option 4: "go above" is not a standard idiomatic phrasal verb in English and does not carry any recognised meaning here.

NOTE

• Other common meanings of "go off": food going off (spoiling), a gun going off (firing), a plan going off well (happening as planned).

• Related phrasal verbs with alarms/devices: "set off the alarm" (to trigger it), "switch off the alarm" (to turn it off).

question:
Identify the incorrectly spelt word and select its correct spelling.
Maybe he wanted to make sure he didn't embarrese her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. embarrass.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Embarrass", to make someone feel awkward, self-conscious, or ashamed.
◦ Example: She didn't want to embarrass her brother in front of his friends.

• Spelling key: EM + BARR (double R) + ASS (double S). The word has two pairs of double letters, "rr" and "ss", which is the most common mistake test-takers make when spelling it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sware" is not a recognised word/spelling and does not relate to the intended word "embarrass".

• Option 2: "shure" is also not a valid English spelling and is unrelated to the tested word.

• Option 4: "emberess" is incorrect; it wrongly changes "barr" to "berr" and drops one "s", distorting both syllables of the correct spelling.

NOTE

• Related word forms: embarrassment (noun), embarrassing (adjective), embarrassed (past participle/adjective).

• Other double letter words commonly misspelt by SSC candidates: occasion, necessary, accommodate, harass, possess, recommend.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The plot of the novel is very dull.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Riveting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Dull" means boring, uninteresting, or lacking excitement. (उबाऊ/नीरस)
◦ Example: The lecture was so dull that half the students fell asleep.

• Its antonym must mean the opposite, something that completely holds one's attention and is extremely interesting, which is exactly what "Riveting" means. (आकर्षक/मनोरम)
◦ Example: The film's plot was so riveting that no one left their seats.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Diverting" means mildly entertaining or amusing; it is a weaker word than "riveting" and does not as strongly capture the opposite of "dull" in the context of gripping a reader's attention.

• Option 3: "Plodding" is incorrect because it is a synonym, not an antonym, of "dull", it describes something slow-moving and tedious.

• Option 4: "Charming" means pleasant or attractive in a personal, charismatic sense; it does not specifically capture the sense of "gripping/exciting" needed to oppose "dull" describing a plot.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "dull" (in this sense): tedious, monotonous, insipid, humdrum, tiresome.

• Other antonyms of "dull": exciting, gripping, captivating, thrilling, engrossing.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that collocates with 'wish' to fill in the blank.
The genie asked Aladdin to _________ a wish.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. make.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct fixed collocation is "make a wish", meaning to silently express a desire for something to happen (often before blowing out candles, throwing a coin in a fountain, etc., or here, when granted a wish by a genie).

• Rule Fixed Collocations: Certain verbs pair conventionally with certain nouns in English and cannot be freely substituted, even by near synonyms. "Wish" always collocates with "make" (make a wish), never with "take", "ask", or "tell".

• Applying the rule: "The genie asked Aladdin to make a wish."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "take" does not collocate with "wish" in standard English; "take" instead pairs with nouns like "a decision", "a photo", "a break".

• Option 3: "ask" is incorrect because "ask a wish" is not a valid English collocation; "ask" typically pairs with "a question" or "a favour".

• Option 4: "tell" is incorrect because "tell" pairs with nouns like "a story" or "a lie", not "a wish".

NOTE

• Other common verb-noun collocations tested by SSC: make a decision, make an effort, take a photo, take a break, ask a favour, tell a lie/story.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Remission
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Pardon.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Remission" means forgiveness or pardon of an offence/sin, or the cancellation/reduction of a debt, penalty, or sentence. (क्षमा/माफी)
◦ Example: The prisoner was granted remission of his sentence for good behaviour.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Pardon", which similarly means an official forgiveness of an offence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Retribution" means punishment inflicted as vengeance for a wrong done; it is nearly opposite in sense to remission, not a synonym.

• Option 3: "Punishment" is also close in meaning to retribution and is the opposite of the forgiveness implied by "remission".

• Option 4: "Overlook" means to fail to notice or to deliberately ignore something; it lacks the formal sense of official forgiveness or reduction of penalty carried by "remission".

NOTE

• Other meanings of "remission": in medicine, a period during which a disease's symptoms are reduced or absent (e.g. "the cancer is in remission").

• Related words: remit (to cancel a debt/punishment, or to send money), remissible (able to be forgiven).

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part.
You can be sentenced for trespassing on someone else's property.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. entering without permission.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Trespassing" means entering someone's land or property without their permission or legal right to do so. (बिना अनुमति के प्रवेश करना)
◦ Example: The farmer warned the hikers against trespassing on his private land.

• This meaning matches option 2 exactly, since "entering without permission" precisely restates the legal sense of trespassing on property.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "conspiring against others" means secretly planning something harmful with others; this describes a completely different offence (conspiracy), not trespassing.

• Option 3: "leaving without permission" is incorrect because trespassing concerns unauthorised entry, not departure.

• Option 4: "showing unselfish devotion" describes selflessness or loyalty, which has no relation to the legal concept of trespassing.

NOTE

• Related legal/one-word substitution terms often tested by SSC: intrude (to enter without invitation), encroach (to gradually intrude on someone's territory/rights), squatter (one who occupies property without legal right).

• Noun form: "trespass" (both the act and the legal offence); "trespasser" (the person who trespasses).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
Let us assume that we will do the job honestly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. think.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Assume" means to suppose or take something to be true without proof, i.e. to think or believe something for the sake of argument. (मान लेना/समझ लेना)
◦ Example: Let us assume that the train will arrive on time.

• Among the given options, "think" is the closest synonym, capturing the sense of supposing or believing something to be the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "allow" means to permit; it does not carry the sense of supposing something to be true.

• Option 3: "take" is too general and does not capture the specific sense of "supposing/believing" carried by "assume" in this context.

• Option 4: "give" means to hand over or provide; it has no semantic overlap with "assume".

NOTE

• Other meanings of "assume": to take on a responsibility or role (e.g. "assume office", "assume control").

• Related word: "assumption" (noun), a thing that is accepted as true without proof, e.g. "a false assumption".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She could easily eat the _________ biryani by herself.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. whole.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word meaning entire/complete, describing the full amount of biryani, the correct word is "whole".

• Rule Homophones: "Whole", "haul", "hall", and "hole" belong to a set of words that sound similar (near homophones) but have entirely different spellings and meanings. Only "whole" fits the intended sense of "entire" here.

• Applying the rule: "She could easily eat the whole biryani by herself.", meaning she could finish the complete dish alone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "haul" means to pull or drag something with effort, or a quantity of something obtained (e.g. "a haul of fish"); it does not fit the sense of "entire".

• Option 3: "hall" refers to a large room or passageway in a building; it is unrelated to quantity.

• Option 4: "hole" refers to a hollow opening or gap; it is unrelated in meaning and only similar in sound to "whole".

NOTE

• Commonly confused sound-alike word sets tested by SSC: whole/hole, haul/hall, allowed/aloud, cereal/serial, principal/principle.

• Remember: "whole" = entire/complete (adjective), while "hole" = an opening or gap (noun).

question:
Select the option that rectifies the spelling of the underlined word in the given sentence.
It has been a usual ocurrence for a few days now.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. occurrence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Occurrence", an incident or event that happens.
◦ Example: Power cuts have become a common occurrence in this area during summer.

• Spelling key: OC + CUR (double R) + RENCE. The word doubles the "r" (occu-rr-ence) and ends in "-ence", not "-ance" or a single "r".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "occerrence" is incorrect; it wrongly changes "occu" to "occe" in the first syllable.

• Option 2: "occurrance" is incorrect; it wrongly uses the ending "-ance" instead of the correct "-ence".

• Option 3: "occurence" is incorrect; it drops one of the two "r"s required in the word.

NOTE

• Related word forms: occur (verb), occurring (present participle, also doubles the "r"), recurrence (a similar word meaning happening again).

• Other commonly misspelt "-rrence/-rrance" words: deterrence, concurrence (correctly end in "-ence"), while words like insurance, appearance, disturbance correctly end in "-ance", there is no shortcut; each word's ending must be memorised individually.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No improvement required'.
We set up on the journey early in the morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. set off.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct phrasal verb for beginning a journey is "set off (on)", not "set up on".

• Rule Fixed Phrasal Verb: "Set off" means to begin a journey or a course of action. "Set up", by contrast, means to establish, arrange, or prepare something (e.g. "set up a business/a tent"), which does not fit the context of starting a journey.

• Applying the rule: "We set off on the journey early in the morning."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "set in" is incorrect because it means (of something unwelcome) to begin and seem likely to continue, e.g. "winter set in", unrelated to starting a journey.

• Option 3: "No improvement required" is incorrect because "set up on" is not idiomatically correct in this context and does need correction.

• Option 4: "set about" is incorrect because it means to begin doing a task (e.g. "set about cleaning the house"), and is not used with "journey" in this fixed sense; "set off on a journey" is the standard idiomatic form.

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs with "set" commonly tested by SSC: set aside (to save for later), set back (to delay/cost someone money), set out (to begin a journey or undertaking, similar to "set off"), set up (to establish/arrange).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word given in the bracket to fill in the blank.
The State media houses present ______ (vociferous) views compared to private media.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. mild.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Vociferous" means expressing opinions or feelings in a loud, forceful, and insistent manner. (ज़ोरदार/उग्र स्वर वाला)
◦ Example: The protestors were vociferous in their demand for justice.

• Its antonym must describe views expressed in a calm, gentle, and restrained manner, which is exactly the meaning of "mild". (नरम/शांत)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "political" relates to government or public affairs; it describes a subject matter, not the manner or intensity of expressing an opinion, so it cannot be the antonym.

• Option 2: "biased" means showing unfair favour towards one side; it describes fairness (or the lack of it), not loudness, so it is not opposite to "vociferous".

• Option 4: "assertive" means confidently stating an opinion; it is close in force to "vociferous" rather than being its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "vociferous": loud, clamorous, strident, boisterous, noisy.

• Other antonyms of "vociferous": quiet, subdued, restrained, reticent, soft-spoken.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Few people turned up to attend the tawdry promo of the new movie.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Elegant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Tawdry" means showy or gaudy but cheap and of low quality; lacking in good taste. (भड़कीला पर सस्ता/भोंडा)
◦ Example: The shop sold tawdry jewellery that looked expensive but fell apart within days.

• Its antonym must mean tasteful, refined, and graceful, which is exactly the sense of "Elegant". (सुरुचिपूर्ण/शालीन)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Showy" is incorrect because it is a synonym, not an antonym, of "tawdry", both describe something flashy or ostentatious.

• Option 3: "Inferior" is incorrect because it is close in sense to "tawdry" (which itself implies low/cheap quality), rather than being its opposite.

• Option 4: "Gawdy" (Gaudy) is incorrect because it is also a synonym of "tawdry", both mean excessively bright or showy in a tasteless way.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "tawdry": gaudy, garish, cheap, flashy, tacky, vulgar.

• Other antonyms of "tawdry": tasteful, refined, sophisticated, classy, dignified.
